plan.topic: Why some people lose less on GLP-1: response patterns in large matched cohorts, and SELECT predictors of weight loss
plan.angle: 'Losing less than your friend? Response varies, and that's in the data.' Slide 2: trial averages with placebo-adjusted vs raw labelled. Slide 3: the five response patterns from the 10,339-pair tirzepatide/semaglutide real-world cohort (high, moderate, late, minimal, regain), definitions copied verbatim, labelled 'observational · EHR data'. Slide 4: from SELECT (Nature Medicine 2024; adults ≥45 with established cardiovascular disease and overweight/obesity, without diabetes): 'weight loss ranged from none to marked; about 1 in 4 lost ≥15%'. Add only factors the paper itself reports. Slide 5: 'benefits can show up beyond the scale': blood pressure, A1C (% and mmol/mol), heart-risk markers. SELECT's Diabetes Care analysis found glycemic benefit even with <2% weight loss. Slide 6: protein, strength training, sleep, fibre. Slide 7: prescriber questions. No switching or dosing talk, a source tag on every claim slide, and the exact prescriber line.

plan.why: A persistent 'Ozempic not working' search, refreshed with the 24 Sep SELECT predictors paper and the 27 Sep coverage. It's a reassuring framework people save and share. | fact-check: The matched-cohort paper appears to be 'Weight-loss dynamics with tirzepatide versus semaglutide' (PubMed 42311474; medRxiv preprint 10.64898/2025.11.30.25341294). It had 10,339 propensity-matched pairs (tirzepatide vs semaglutide, EHR data) and defines FIVE categories, not four: high (>15% loss), moderate (5–15%), late (<5% in year 1 but >5% cumulative by year 2), minimal (<5%), and weight regain (>5% loss in year 1 then >5% regain in year 2). Check the journal and year on the published version, and show all five. I could not verify a SELECT 'predictors of weight loss' paper in Diabetes Care. The SELECT Diabetes Care paper (2024) is about glycemia regression/progression. The SELECT weight-loss heterogeneity paper is Ryan et al., Nature Medicine 2024: weight loss ranged from none to marked, about a quarter lost ≥15%, and meaningful loss was seen across sexes, races, body sizes and regions. It has been referred to for predictors, but check which factors it actually reports before listing any. SELECT population: adults ≥45 with BMI ≥27, established cardiovascular disease, and no diabetes. Observational real-world predictors (e.g., PubMed 42248359: diabetes, older age, Hispanic ethnicity linked to less loss) must be labelled as associations and handled without stigma.

package.title: Losing Less on a GLP-1? What Response Patterns Research Shows

social.facebook_caption:
Ever wonder why two people on the same GLP-1 medicine can have really different results on the scale? Turns out, response varies, and it's in the data.

In the big trials, average weight loss on the highest doses ranged from about 9.6% to 20.9% over 68–72 weeks, depending on the drug and whether people had type 2 diabetes (placebo groups lost 2.4–3.4%). Averages hide a wide spread. In an observational study of US health records (10,339 matched tirzepatide–semaglutide pairs followed for 2 years), researchers found 5 response patterns: high, moderate, late, minimal, and weight regain — some people lost little in year 1 but more by year 2. The study couldn't fully account for dose, adherence or other medicines. These patterns describe groups, not your future. The scale isn't the whole story either: in the SELECT trial (adults 45+ with established cardiovascular disease and overweight/obesity, no diabetes), more people on semaglutide reached normal blood sugar at 3 years (69.5% vs 35.8%), and weight loss explained only about a quarter of that.

If you're on a GLP-1 and feeling discouraged by your numbers, what would help you feel more confident talking to your doctor about it?

It's a prescription medicine. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

#GLP1 #WeightLossScience #MetabolicHealth

factcheck.summary:
The carousel is accurate and safe. The key numbers check out against the trial results, and I confirmed seven of the eleven sources directly. STEP 1 (−14.9% vs −2.4%, a 12.4-point difference, 68 weeks), SURMOUNT-1 (−20.9% vs −3.1%, 17.8 points, highest-dose arm, 72 weeks), STEP 2 (9.6%, placebo 3.4%) and SURMOUNT-2 (14.7%, placebo 3.2%) all match. The placebo range of 2.4–3.4% is right, and the trial populations are named correctly.

I confirmed the PNAS Nexus 2026 paper (published 16 June 2026): 10,339 matched pairs, US academic health-system medical records, 2-year follow-up, and the five response groups as defined on slide 3.

The Diabetes Care SELECT analysis shows 69.5% vs 35.8% reaching normal blood sugar at 156 weeks, with weight loss explaining about 24.5–27.1% of the effect, so "about a quarter" is fair. SELECT's population, the 20% relative risk reduction (6.5% vs 8.0%), about 3.3 years of follow-up, and lower blood pressure and CRP are right. So are the WHO advice on muscle-strengthening 2+ days a week, CDC's 7+ hours of sleep, and the 2025 joint nutrition advisory.

Framing is good throughout: raw vs placebo-adjusted numbers are labeled, the observational data is flagged, "separate trials" is noted, and relative risk comes with absolute numbers. The prescriber line is exact.

Five small wording fixes:
1. Slide 3 should say the real-world group included people with and without type 2 diabetes. Otherwise it reads as the same no-diabetes population as slide 2.
2. Slide 3's regain threshold should read "≥5%".
3. Slide 3 should add the authors' main limitation.
4. Slide 6 needs a protein caveat for people with kidney disease.
5. The SELECT 22.9% figure couldn't be checked against the full text, because the pages were paywalled or blocked by a captcha. It's consistent with other reports, which put it at about 23%.

I haven't listed the four sources I couldn't open: STEP 1, STEP 2, SURMOUNT-1 and SURMOUNT-2. Their figures match the published results, but their DOI links still need a manual click-check.

issues.claim: Observational · EHR data · 10,339 propensity-matched tirzepatide–semaglutide pairs. Patterns describe groups, not your future.
issues.problem: It leaves out who was studied and what the authors say the study can't show. The PNAS Nexus group included people with and without type 2 diabetes, from US academic medical centers, followed for 2 years. Coming right after slide 2 (no diabetes), readers may assume it's the same population. The authors also say the design can't account for dose, adherence, other medicines, or tolerability.
issues.fix: Observational · US health-record data · 10,339 matched tirzepatide–semaglutide pairs, with and without type 2 diabetes, followed 2 years. Couldn't fully account for dose, adherence or other medicines. Patterns describe groups, not your future. Source: Weight-loss dynamics with tirzepatide vs semaglutide, PNAS Nexus 2026.
